The post Top 10 Best Adaptive / Risk-Based Authentication Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Prompting every user for MFA on every login trains people to approve anything, leaving enterprises open to push-bombing and MFA fatigue attacks; challenging nobody invites automated account takeover (ATO) attacks and credential stuffing.

Adaptive authentication resolves the tension score the context, challenge the risky and 2026’s leaders now pair those risk engines with passkeys and token defense. We scored ten tools across workforce and fraud lanes.

Microsoft Conditional Access ranks 1 on policy depth per dollar; Okta and Cisco Duo complete the podium.

Roster note: our source list carried Ping Identity and ForgeRock separately; merged since 2023, they rank once nine distinct vendors, honestly counted.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Microsoft Conditional Access the deepest policy engine most buyers already license.

• Podium: Conditional Access (estate depth), Okta (SaaS-wide risk policy), Duo (fastest pragmatic rollout).

• Two lanes, one label: workforce step-up (Microsoft/Okta/Duo/Ping) and consumer fraud risk (Trusteer, BioCatch, Transmit) are different purchases we rank both, labeled.

• Scoring bias: we rewarded tools that step up into phishing-resistant factors, not into another phishable OTP.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: documented signal breadth (device, network, behavior, threat intel), policy expressiveness, passkey integration, pricing clarity, and deployment evidence.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: signal quality 30%, policy expressiveness 25%, step-up quality 20%, pricing clarity 15%, ecosystem 10%. [VERIFY] flags pre-purchase confirmations.

The 2026 Adaptive Authentication Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1 Microsoft Conditional Access — Best Overall Policy Engine

Snapshot: Bundled; risk features by Entra tier | Signals: identity + device + location + risk | Passkey enforcement

Why it earns 1: The richest policy grammar in the market, fed by Identity Protection risk scores, Intune device compliance, and Microsoft’s threat-signal firehose included, at meaningful depth, in licensing most organizations already hold. It pairs with continuous mitigation updates protecting environments against Conditional Access policy bypasses via Nested App Authentication to extend decisions past the initial login moment.

Standout features: Risk-based policies; device-compliance conditions; Identity Protection; session/token controls; passkey requirement policies.

Pros: Bundled; estate-deep signals; mature policy model.

Cons: Full risk scoring gates to P2; Microsoft-estate center of gravity.

Bottom line: For M365 estates, the best adaptive engine is a configuration sprint away.

2 Okta — Best SaaS-Wide Risk Policy

Snapshot: Per-module [VERIFY] | Risk scoring + device assurance | 7,000+ apps covered

Why it earns 2: One risk policy, thousands of app logins: network, device, and velocity signals driving per-app, per-group step-ups, backed by rapid vendor engineering addressing Okta delegated authentication and access flaws, with FastPass and passkeys as the phishing-resistant destination.

Standout features: Risk-scored authentication; device assurance; behavior detection; per-app policies; FastPass integration.

Pros: Catalog-wide reach; granularity.

Cons: Module economics; platform commitment.

Bottom line: The adaptive layer of choice for Okta-anchored estates.

3 Cisco Duo — Best Pragmatic Rollout

Snapshot: Published per-user tiers | Risk-based factor selection | Device health included

Why it earns 3: Adaptive without the identity-program prerequisite: Wi-Fi fingerprint shifts, unusual locations, and attack patterns adjusting challenges dynamically, deployed in weeks at published prices atop Duo’s device-trust base while mitigating vulnerabilities like Cisco Duo authentication bypasses on Windows Logon and RDP.

Standout features: Risk-based authentication; Verified Push escalation; device posture; Trust Monitor; transparent tiers.

Pros: Speed; pricing clarity; posture context.

Cons: Signal depth trails the fraud-lane engines.

Bottom line: The fastest meaningful upgrade from static MFA.

4 Ping Identity (incl. ForgeRock) — Best Orchestrated Risk

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | PingOne Protect + DaVinci | Workforce and CIAM

Why it earns 4: Risk as a journey component: PingOne Protect scores fused with external fraud feeds and custom logic inside DaVinci flows, backed by proactive mitigations for Ping Identity policy enforcement and Java Agent vulnerabilities the tool for enterprises whose step-up decisions live mid-journey, not just at login. Ranked once despite two sheet entries.

Standout features: Risk engine; signal fusion; orchestration; passkey step-ups; hybrid deployment.

Pros: Expressiveness ceiling.

Cons: Identity-engineering prerequisite; quotes.

Bottom line: The orchestration pick for complex, regulated journeys.

5 IBM (Trusteer) — Best Banking-Channel Risk

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | Lane label: fraud, not workforce | Malware/RAT + session risk

Why it earns 5: Decades of financial-malware telemetry feeding channel risk decisions: detecting remote access tools (RATs), automated transaction systems, and threats like ToxicPanda and mobile banking trojans attempting on-device fraud where workforce tools cannot see.

Standout features: Malware/RAT detection; session risk; ATO signals; mobile SDK; banking integrations.

Pros: Channel depth; threat-research lineage.

Cons: Banking-centric; enterprise motion.

Bottom line: The digital-banking risk specialist.

6 BioCatch — Best Behavioral Signals

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | Lane label: fraud monitoring | Typing/swipe/navigation models

Why it earns 6: The signal source others license: behavioral biometrics exposing takeover, mule accounts, and scam-coerced sessions, recognized among the top fraud prevention companies for providing risk intelligence on sessions that already passed login checks.

Standout features: Behavioral profiling; coercion/scam detection; mule detection; real-time scoring; banking traction.

Pros: Catches post-login fraud; unique signal class.

Cons: Fraud-team product; tuning investment.

Bottom line: The behavioral layer for banks serious about scams, not just logins.

7 Transmit Security — Best Passkey-Era Consumer Risk

Snapshot: Quote/usage [VERIFY] | CIAM + fraud fusion | Detection-and-response services

Why it earns 7: Consumer authentication and risk decisioning designed together: passkeys, device intelligence, and fraud detection in one platform, ranked among the leading Customer Identity and Access Management (CIAM) solutions for moving millions of users to low-friction, risk-scored sign-ins.

Standout features: Risk decisioning; passkey flows; device intelligence; identity verification; developer APIs.

Pros: Modern consumer stack; fraud fusion.

Cons: Enterprise motion; packaging clarity.

Bottom line: The consumer-scale pick for passkey-first risk.

8 RSA — Best Regulated-Estate Continuity

Snapshot: ID Plus tiers/quote [VERIFY] | Risk engine heritage | SecurID estate integration

Why it earns 8: The adaptive layer for organizations already running RSA: risk-based authentication woven into SecurID estates and ID Plus cloud, evaluated across the top user access management tools to modernize regulated deployments without rip-and-replace.

Standout features: Risk engine; token + modern factor mix; ID Plus cloud; governance ties; on-prem depth.

Pros: Continuity; compliance familiarity.

Cons: Rarely the greenfield choice; momentum.

Bottom line: The modernization path for RSA shops.

9 SecureAuth — Best Flexible Mid-Enterprise

Snapshot: Per-user/quote [VERIFY] | Arculix risk engine | Passwordless continuum

Why it earns 9: The flexible specialist: Arculix’s device-trust and behavioral scoring driving step-ups across VPNs, legacy apps, and SaaS, featured among top Single Sign-On (SSO) providers with risk-based adaptive MFA for mid-enterprises that find anchor platforms rigid.

Standout features: Risk scoring; device trust; passwordless flows; broad protocol support; policy granularity.

Pros: Flexibility; legacy reach.

Cons: Smaller vendor; ecosystem breadth.

Bottom line: The tailor-made option when the big platforms’ policies don’t fit.

Consolidated: ForgeRock — Ranked Within Ping (4)

ForgeRock’s adaptive and journey tooling sells under Ping Identity since the 2023 merger. Separate rankings double-count one vendor — we didn’t.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Tune by the Only Metric That Matters

Deploy the bundled engine first, then measure challenge-rate versus fraud-caught the single tuning metric that keeps adaptive honest. Route high-risk events to passkeys or verification, never to another OTP.

Remember what login-time scoring cannot prevent on its own: stolen session tokens skip authentication entirely.

Organizations must implement CISA and NIST guidelines for identity token security and token binding to validate cryptographic bindings throughout the session lifecycle, supplemented by continuous monitoring tools that catch session anomalies post-auth.

FAQs

What is the best adaptive authentication tool in 2026? Microsoft Conditional Access ranks 1 on policy depth for M365 estates; Okta leads SaaS-wide risk policy; Duo wins pragmatic rollout; Ping (with ForgeRock) tops orchestration; Trusteer, BioCatch, and Transmit lead the consumer-fraud lane.

What is risk-based authentication? Authentication that adjusts dynamically to context device health, location, network, behavior, and threat intelligence.

Low-risk logins flow smoothly; anomalies trigger step-up or block. This risk-adaptive model forms the bedrock of modern passwordless authentication and FIDO2 adoption.

Is adaptive authentication the same as MFA? No MFA supplies the factors; adaptive decides when to demand them. The 2026 pattern: passkeys as the factor, risk signals as the trigger, identity verification as the top escalation.

Do workforce and customer authentication need different tools? Usually workforce engines (Conditional Access, Okta, Duo) read device compliance and directory context; fraud engines (Trusteer, BioCatch) read malware signals and behavioral patterns across millions of consumer sessions. Same vocabulary, different buyers and budgets.

Does adaptive authentication stop session hijacking? Not alone token theft bypasses login-time scoring. Add token binding, continuous session evaluation, and behavioral monitoring for post-login coverage; several ranked vendors now ship exactly that combination.

Verdict

Conditional Access takes 2026 on depth-per-dollar, Okta and Duo make adaptive practical everywhere else, and the fraud lane Trusteer, BioCatch, Transmit guards the customers your workforce tools never see. Challenge less, verify better, and let passkeys be where every escalation lands.

articles.description:

We scored ten vendors with liveness and injection-attack defense weighted highest, because that’s where fraud actually breaks through. iProov ranks #1 on […]

The post Top 10 Best Biometric Authentication Solutions in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Matching a face got easy; proving the face is a live human at a real camera while generative AI mass-produces convincing deepfake threats is where the modern biometric authentication market earns its keep.

We scored ten vendors with liveness and injection-attack defense weighted highest, because that’s where fraud actually breaks through. iProov ranks #1 on attack-defense science; BioCatch and Entrust (Onfido) complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: iProov the deepest defense against presentation and injection attacks, proven in government deployments.

• Podium: iProov (liveness science), BioCatch (post-login behavioral defense), Entrust/Onfido (portfolio-scale onboarding).

• Two different jobs: verification biometrics (login/onboarding) and behavioral biometrics for account takeover defense share a word, not a purchase.

• The 2026 criterion: injection-attack defense deepfakes fed through virtual cameras separates leaders from matchers.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: documented liveness/PAD approaches, certification participation (iBeta/NIST), production scale, privacy architecture, and deployment reports.

No lab testing by us; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: liveness/injection defense 30%, accuracy evidence 20%, scale/production proof 20%, privacy architecture 15%, integration breadth 15%. [VERIFY] flags pre-purchase confirmations.

The 2026 Biometric Authentication Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1 iProov — Best Liveness & Injection Defense

Snapshot: Quote/volume [VERIFY] | Flashmark genuine-presence tech | Gov/border deployments

Why it earns 1: The question is no longer “is this the right face” but “is there a live human at a real camera at all” and iProov’s patented illumination science plus a dedicated threat-intelligence unit defend against presentation attack detection gaps and synthetic injection attacks. National-scale government deployments back the claim.

Standout features: Genuine presence assurance; injection-attack defense; threat intelligence; cloud delivery; accessibility focus.

Pros: Attack-defense depth; deployment pedigree.

Cons: Verification lane, not full KYC suite; quotes.

Bottom line: Where deepfakes are the threat model, this is the shortlist’s top line.

2 BioCatch — Best Behavioral Fraud Defense

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | Behavioral biometrics | Banking fraud focus lane label: monitoring, not login

Why it earns 2: The strongest answer to fraud that survives authentication: typing rhythm, swipe dynamics, and navigation patterns exposing account takeover and credential exploitation campaigns in real time. A session can pass every login check and still be a crime in progress; behavior tells.

Standout features: Behavioral profiling; ATO detection; scam/coercion signals; mule detection; banking integrations.

Pros: Catches what login can’t; deep banking traction.

Cons: Fraud-team product with tuning investment; not an authenticator.

Bottom line: The post-login guard the verification vendors don’t sell.

3 Entrust (Onfido) — Best Portfolio Onboarding

Snapshot: Per-verification/volume [VERIFY] | Document + selfie + liveness | Entrust portfolio

Why it earns 3: KYC-grade onboarding thousands of ID types, selfie match, fraud signals now inside Entrust’s certificate-rooted identity and PKI infrastructure, giving enterprises one large vendor for verification, credentials, and PKI. Buy under current Entrust packaging.

Standout features: Document authenticity; selfie + liveness; workflow studio; global coverage; portfolio integration.

Pros: Breadth + vendor stability.

Cons: Post-acquisition SKU evolution. [VERIFY]

Bottom line: The enterprise-consolidation pick for verified onboarding.

4 Aware — Best Biometric Software Toolkit

Snapshot: SDK/platform licensing [VERIFY] | AwareID + ABIS components | Decades of NIST participation

Why it earns 4: The veteran toolkit vendor: face/fingerprint/voice engines, liveness, and an ABIS platform sold as software components and the AwareID cloud service letting enterprises assemble biometric capabilities within enterprise identity and access management architectures without mega-vendor lock-in.

Standout features: AwareID cloud onboarding/auth; matching engines; liveness; ABIS platform; standards participation.

Pros: Component flexibility; long federal/enterprise record.

Cons: Brand quieter than consumer-facing rivals; assembly required.

Bottom line: The build-it-your-way alternative to turnkey verification suites.

5 FaceTec — Best 3D Liveness Technology

Snapshot: SDK licensing [VERIFY] | 3D face maps | Spoof-bounty program

Why it earns 5: The 3D-liveness specialist whose SDK powers verification flows across hundreds of platforms depth-mapped face capture defending against AI-generated spoof attacks and a public bounty program that puts money behind its claims.

Standout features: 3D face mapping; certified liveness; server-side matching; SDK delivery; bounty-tested defenses.

Pros: Technology depth; embed flexibility.

Cons: Component vendor you build the product around it.

Bottom line: The engine of choice for teams building verification in-house.

6 Daon — Best Omnichannel Platform

Snapshot: Platform/quote [VERIFY] | IdentityX/TrustX | Face/voice/behavior in one

Why it earns 6: The multi-modal orchestrator: face, voice, document, and behavioral factors managed across mobile, web, and call-center channels from one platform, supporting omnichannel enterprise identity orchestration across banking and telecommunications.

Standout features: Multi-modal orchestration; omnichannel coverage; TrustX workflows; long banking/telco record.

Pros: Channel breadth; deployment maturity.

Cons: Brand quieter than rivals; platform framing.

Bottom line: One platform when your biometrics must span app, web, and phone line.

7 HID Global — Best Physical-Logical Convergence

Snapshot: Hardware + licensing/quote [VERIFY] | Readers to platform | Badge-to-desktop

Why it earns 7: The only ranked vendor treating the door and the login as one program: fingerprint/face readers, credential ecosystems, and converged authentication and access control solutions unifying building security with workstation authentication.

Standout features: Biometric readers; credential management; FIDO ties; access-control integration.

Pros: Convergence breadth; hardware maturity.

Cons: Hardware-project gravity; not a KYC play.

Bottom line: The facilities-plus-IT unification pick.

8 Veridas — Best Voice Biometric & Anti-Spoofing Engine

Snapshot: Enterprise/OEM licensing [VERIFY] | Voice biometrics + anti-spoofing | Identity verification platform

Why it earns 8: Veridas combines voice biometrics with anti-spoofing capabilities to help organizations authenticate users through their voice while detecting deepfake threats in authentication and verification systems. Its technology can be integrated into authentication and identity-verification workflows rather than requiring organizations to build a biometric engine from scratch.

Standout features: Voice biometrics; voice authentication; anti-spoofing; deepfake/synthetic-voice detection; SDK/API integration.

Pros: Strong voice-security focus; embeddable technology; supports authentication and fraud-prevention workflows.

Cons: More specialized than a full turnkey identity platform; enterprise deployment and pricing require verification.

Bottom line: A strong component-oriented choice for organizations and platform providers looking to embed voice biometrics and anti-spoofing into authentication or identity-verification workflows.

9 Microsoft (Nuance) — Best Voice/Contact-Center

Snapshot: Enterprise/quote [VERIFY] | Gatekeeper voice biometrics | Contact-center native

Why it earns 9: The call center is the fraud channel biometrics forgot and Nuance Gatekeeper authenticates callers by voice while flagging fraudsters and synthetic speech, countering AI-fueled impersonation and social engineering campaigns targeting enterprise service desks.

Standout features: Voice authentication; fraudster watchlists; synthetic-speech detection; contact-center integration.

Pros: Channel depth; Microsoft scale.

Cons: Voice-channel focus; enterprise motion.

Bottom line: The phone-channel answer as deepfake voice attacks climb.

10 Fingerprint Cards — Best Sensor Hardware Lane

Snapshot: OEM hardware | Lane label: sensors, not software platform | Devices/cards/access

Why it earns 10: The Swedish sensor maker inside phones, laptops, access systems, and biometric payment cards. Its hardware modules power biometric sensors on devices transitioning to passkeys and passwordless hardware authenticators.

Standout features: Capacitive/optical sensors; biometric payment cards; access hardware; OEM ecosystem.

Pros: Hardware pedigree; embedded reach.

Cons: Not an enterprise auth solution; OEM sales motion.

Bottom line: Hardware-lane entry ranked for completeness, bought by device makers.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Name the Job First

“Biometric authentication” hides four purchases: onboarding verification (Entrust, with FaceTec/ID R&D inside builders’ stacks), high-assurance login defense (iProov), post-login fraud monitoring (BioCatch, Nuance for voice), and components/hardware (Aware, FaceTec, ID R&D, HID, Fingerprint Cards).

Buy by job, demand injection-attack evidence in every lane, and ensure your identity enrollment architecture adheres strictly to GDPR compliance and privacy standards as well as Illinois BIPA guidelines regulatory fines and class-action penalties for non-consensual biometric processing outrun software license fees every time.

FAQs

What is the best biometric authentication solution in 2026? iProov ranks 1 for liveness and injection-attack defense; BioCatch leads post-login behavioral fraud detection; Entrust (Onfido) tops portfolio onboarding; Aware leads software toolkits. The job onboarding, login, monitoring, or components picks the vendor.

Can biometrics be fooled by deepfakes? Weak implementations, yes which is why injection-attack defense (detecting synthesized streams fed through virtual cameras) is 2026’s deciding criterion.

Ask vendors for specific injection-attack testing evidence, not just presentation-attack certificates.

What’s the difference between verification and behavioral biometrics? Verification proves identity at a moment face plus liveness at login or onboarding.

Behavioral biometrics monitors how a user types and navigates throughout a session to catch takeover or coercion. A lock versus a guard; mature programs deploy both.

Are biometrics legally risky? Mishandled, very: GDPR treats biometric data as special-category, and Illinois BIPA attaches per-violation damages to consent failures.

Architect explicit consent, minimal retention, and encrypted templates before launch privacy design is part of the product.

Should biometrics replace passwords entirely? Pair rather than replace: deploy passkeys and passwordless authentication (where device biometrics unlock cryptographic keys) for day-to-day login, server-side verification biometrics for high-assurance moments, and behavioral monitoring post-login.

Verdict

iProov takes 2026 on the science that matters most, BioCatch guards the session everyone else forgets, and Entrust consolidates onboarding at portfolio scale. Rank your fraud losses by channel, match the lane, and let injection-attack evidence not demo-day accuracy break the ties.

articles.description:
Nobody gets promoted for building login, but plenty get breached maintaining it. Authentication-as-a-Service moved from convenience to best practice: passkeys, attack protection, and compliance maintained by vendors whose whole business is sign-in. Integrating modern AaaS with established Customer Identity and Access Management (CIAM) solutions has cemented Identity and Access Management (IAM) resilience as a CISO […]

The post Top 10 Best Authentication-as-a-Service (AaaS) Providers in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Nobody gets promoted for building login, but plenty get breached maintaining it. Authentication-as-a-Service moved from convenience to best practice: passkeys, attack protection, and compliance maintained by vendors whose whole business is sign-in.

Integrating modern AaaS with established Customer Identity and Access Management (CIAM) solutions has cemented Identity and Access Management (IAM) resilience as a CISO priority across modern cloud architectures.

We scored ten providers on developer experience, security depth, and the MAU economics that decide the real winner at scale.

Auth0 ranks #1; Microsoft Entra External ID and Firebase Auth complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Auth0 (Okta’s developer line) still the benchmark, still the procurement fast-pass.

• Podium: Auth0 (ecosystem), Entra External ID (price floor), Firebase Auth (prototype-to-scale reach).

• Insurgent lanes are real: Stytch (fraud-fused), Descope (visual flows), SuperTokens (open source), FusionAuth (self-host) each beat the giants on their home turf.

• The MAU curve is the decision: free floors flatter everyone; year-three volumes reveal the true ranking for your product.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: SDK/documentation quality, passkey and attack-protection depth, published pricing and free floors, scale/sovereignty options, and developer-community signal.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: developer experience 25%, security depth 25%, pricing/free-floor economics 20%, scale evidence 15%, ecosystem 15%. [VERIFY] flags pre-purchase confirmations.

The 2026 AaaS Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1 Auth0 (Okta) — Best Overall

Snapshot: Per-MAU, free dev tier | Passkeys + attack protection | One vendor with Okta

Why it earns 1: The reference implementation of outsourced login: Universal Login, SDKs for everything, marketplace extensibility, and compliance attestations that make enterprise security reviews a formality.

Platform teams also benefit from vendor security updates addressing vulnerabilities in Auth0 connectors and gateways to protect underlying user directories. Ownership note for clean procurement: Auth0 is Okta’s developer product line.

Standout features: Universal Login; passkeys; actions/extensibility; B2B organizations; bot detection.

Pros: Ecosystem, docs, credibility.

Cons: MAU curve at scale; tier-gated features.

Bottom line: The default that competitors must beat on economics or lane fit not on capability.

2 Microsoft Entra External ID — Best Price Floor

Snapshot: Published per-MAU, large free allowance [VERIFY] | Azure-native | B2C successor

Why it earns 2: The economics headline: a free MAU allowance most startups never exhaust, governed with Azure-familiar tooling, paired with Conditional Access enforcement preventing authentication bypass attacks. Passkeys and custom journeys have matured enough to make this the value anchor for Microsoft-committed teams.

Standout features: Free allowance; custom journeys; social/passkeys; Azure integration; compliance surface.

Pros: Price floor; bundle gravity.

Cons: Journey learning curve; migration nuances from B2C.

Bottom line: Price this first if you’re anywhere near Azure.

3 Firebase Auth (Google) — Best Prototype-to-Scale

Snapshot: Free tier + Identity Platform usage pricing | Mobile-first | GCP-wired

Why it earns #3: The fastest zero-to-login in the industry, and no longer just for prototypes: Identity Platform upgrades add SAML/OIDC, MFA, and multi-tenancy when businesses arrive, provided teams follow best practices for securing Firebase endpoints and database authentication rules to prevent data leakage. Mobile-first products stay for the SDK ubiquity.

Standout features: Email/social/phone auth; Identity Platform tier; SDK breadth; generous free usage; GCP integration.

Pros: Free floor; platform fit; Google scale.

Cons: Deep B2B/custom needs arrive late; GCP gravity.

Bottom line: The pragmatic start that scales further than its reputation suggests.

4 Amazon Cognito — Best AWS-Native Value

Snapshot: Published per-MAU, generous free tier | Lambda-extensible | IAM-wired

Why it earns #4: The cheapest serious floor in the ranking, wired into the AWS your team already operates. Managed login pages and passkey support narrowed the old UX complaints; Lambda triggers still handle custom authentication challenges while mitigating AWS IAM authentication enumeration vulnerabilities across web console entry points.

Standout features: Free-tier floor; Lambda triggers; user pools/federation; AWS integration; managed UI.

Pros: Cost; AWS fit.

Cons: DX still trails Auth0; assembly for advanced flows.

Bottom line: AWS-native products need a reason not to use it.

5 Stytch — Best Fraud-Fused APIs

Snapshot: Free tier; per-MAU/usage [VERIFY] | Device fingerprinting built in | B2B suite

Why it earns #5: Login and abuse defense as one API surface passkeys, magic links, device fingerprinting, and bot detection designed for real-time bot detection and account takeover protection. Products that succeed attract fraud; Stytch prices that reality in from the start.

Standout features: Passkeys/magic links; fingerprinting; bot detection; B2B organizations; session management.

Pros: Fraud signals included; modern DX.

Cons: Ecosystem younger than Auth0’s.

Bottom line: The security-forward pick for abuse-exposed consumer and B2B apps.

6 Descope — Best No/Low-Code Flows

Snapshot: Generous free tier; per-MAU [VERIFY] | Visual workflow builder | Passkey-first

Why it earns 6: Authentication as flowchart: drag-and-drop journeys, passkey-first templates, and rework-without-redeploy iteration that keeps product teams out of auth code permanently. Its engineering pedigree is demonstrated by Descope research exposing the nOAuth authentication flaw to prevent account takeovers in cross-tenant environments.

Standout features: Visual flow editor; passkeys/WebAuthn; MFA step-ups; fraud signals; B2B tenants.

Pros: Speed; free floor; flow flexibility.

Cons: Younger vendor diligence.

Bottom line: The fastest passkey-first ship for teams that think in flows.

7 FusionAuth — Best Self-Host Control

Snapshot: Published tiers; community self-host | Standards-complete | Deployment freedom

Why it earns 7: The per-MAU escape hatch: full-featured auth you can self-host with unlimited users, converting login cost into infrastructure. Evaluated among the top developer-focused passwordless authentication platforms, it attracts data-locality and cost-certainty buyers deliberately.

Standout features: Self-host or cloud; OAuth/OIDC/SAML; passkeys; multi-tenant; published pricing.

Pros: Cost control; sovereignty; docs.

Cons: You operate it (or pay for its cloud).

Bottom line: When the MAU math or the residency clause bites, this is the exit.

8 Frontegg — Best B2B Feature Suite

Snapshot: Per-MAU/tiers [VERIFY] | Per-tenant SSO/SCIM | Customer-facing admin portals

Why it earns #8: The enterprise-readiness checklist productized: self-service portals offering enterprise Single Sign-On (SSO) and SAML federation, automated SCIM provisioning, roles, and audit logs that turn B2B deal blockers into instant configuration.

Standout features: Tenant SSO/SCIM; admin portals; entitlements; audit logs; SDKs.

Pros: B2B velocity; deal-unblocking.

Cons: Costs scale with tenant count; younger vendor.

Bottom line: The B2B specialist that pays for itself at the first enterprise contract.

9 Ping Identity — Best Orchestrated Enterprise

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | DaVinci orchestration | Hybrid options

Why it earns #9: Above a complexity threshold regulated journeys, merged user bases, fraud-signal fusion hosted auth becomes orchestration. Ping’s DaVinci remains that lane’s deepest tool, supported by enterprise mitigations for enterprise identity orchestration and policy enforcement across complex hybrid environments.

Standout features: Hosted auth; DaVinci flows; risk integration; passkeys; CIAM scale.

Pros: Journey ceiling.

Cons: Not a startup product; enterprise economics.

Bottom line: The enterprise-complexity answer, priced accordingly.

10 SuperTokens — Best Open-Source Challenger

Snapshot: OSS core; published managed tiers [VERIFY] | Self-host free | Recipe-based SDKs

Why it earns #10: The open-source insurgent: robust session management designed to enforce session token binding and secure session management to prevent token hijacking, recipe-style SDKs, and a self-host lane at zero license cost the credible budget-and-control alternative for engineering-led startups.

Standout features: OSS core; pre-built recipes; session security; self-host or managed; growing passkey support.

Pros: OSS economics; control; momentum.

Cons: Feature breadth and ecosystem trail the leaders.

Bottom line: Watch-and-adopt for teams that want Auth0 outcomes at OSS prices.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Run the Year-Three Numbers

Model three scenarios before any signature: your launch MAUs (everyone’s free), your success-case MAUs (where Auth0 and Entra diverge sharply), and your breakout-case MAUs (where self-host FusionAuth/SuperTokens or Cognito’s floor wins outright).

Then verify the exit architecture: audit export paths, password-hash portability, standard protocols, and integrate API security testing and protection tools to ensure auth endpoints are defended against automated abuse. Vendor lock-in is real precisely because switching authentication engines is risky at scale test the door before entering the room.

FAQs

What is the best authentication-as-a-service provider in 2026? Auth0 ranks #1 on ecosystem and enterprise credibility; Entra External ID wins the price floor for Azure teams; Firebase and Cognito anchor platform-native value; Stytch and Descope lead the modern insurgent lanes.

How much does AaaS actually cost? Free floors are generous across the board; per-MAU pricing above them diverges wildly at scale. The honest comparison is your year-three success scenario, not the pricing page’s first tier.

Is outsourced authentication secure? Generally more secure than homegrown: dedicated teams maintain passkey ceremonies, attack protection, and compliance continuously. Residual duties stay yours recovery flows, session policy, monitoring, and vendor incident-history diligence.

When does self-hosting auth make sense? When per-MAU fees exceed infrastructure-plus-engineering cost, under data-sovereignty mandates, or for unusual customization FusionAuth and SuperTokens exist for exactly that graduation, with real engineering ownership as the price.

Do all AaaS providers support passkeys? Every ranked provider ships or is shipping passkey flows as organizations prioritize transitioning users away from passwords to passkeys. Differentiation moved to migration tooling converting existing password users and fraud-signal depth around the ceremony.

Verdict

Auth0 keeps the crown, Entra External ID presses on price, Firebase and Cognito own their platforms’ gravity and the insurgents win their lanes outright. The real ranking is produced by your MAU spreadsheet and your stack; our scores just tell you who to model first.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Every domain controller still humming in a server closet is a patch cycle, an attack surface, and a reminder that identity hasn’t finished moving to the cloud.

We scored the leading cloud directories on identity depth, protocol coverage, device integration, and pricing clarity. In modern environments adopting Single Sign-On (SSO) solutions, Microsoft Entra ID ranks #1 on sheer gravitational pull; JumpCloud and Okta Universal Directory complete the podium.

Roster note: our source list carried Ping Identity and ForgeRock separately; they merged in 2023 and sell as one platform, so we rank them once nine distinct vendors, honestly counted.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Microsoft Entra ID the directory most organizations are already migrating into, whether they planned to or not.

• Podium: Entra (bundle gravity), JumpCloud (best domainless package), Okta UD (best neutral hub).

• Lane clarity wins: AWS Directory Service hosts AD-dependent workloads; it is not your workforce directory buyers confuse these constantly.

• Protocol check: RADIUS and LDAP needs sink more cutovers than any feature gap Foxpass and JumpCloud own that floor.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based: documentation, protocol coverage (LDAP/RADIUS/SCIM), mobile device management (MDM) integration, published pricing, and practitioner migration reports. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Weights: identity/lifecycle depth 25%, protocol coverage 25%, device integration 20%, pricing clarity 15%, migration tooling 15%. [VERIFY] flags pre-purchase confirmations.

The 2026 Cloud Directory Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1 Microsoft Entra ID — Best Overall

Snapshot: Bundled with M365 | Hybrid sync from AD | Conditional Access + Intune pairing

Why it earns 1: The migration destination of record. Hybrid sync absorbs AD estates gradually, Conditional Access turns the directory into a policy engine, and cloud Kerberos plus passkeys sketch the road to the last domain controller’s retirement utilizing Microsoft Intune and Entra ID integration to verify device identities directly via certificate-bound trust chains.

Standout features: Hybrid sync; Conditional Access; Intune device trust; app gallery; cloud Kerberos/passkeys.

Pros: Bundle economics; deepest Windows path; published tiers.

Cons: LDAP/RADIUS needs companions; cross-OS depth varies via Intune.

Bottom line: For Microsoft-licensed estates, the question is sequencing, not selection.

2 JumpCloud — Best Domainless Package

Snapshot: Published per-user tiers + free tier | Cloud LDAP/RADIUS native | Mac/Windows/Linux MDM

Why it earns 2: The most complete answer to “run a company without domain controllers”: directory, SSO, MFA, cloud RADIUS/LDAP, and cross-OS device management in one console, supported by regular security hardening across JumpCloud’s unified directory, device management, and SSO platform.

Standout features: Cloud LDAP/RADIUS; cross-OS device management; SSO/MFA; HR-sync; conditional access.

Pros: One-console breadth; protocol floor covered; pricing transparency.

Cons: Enterprise federation ceilings; app catalog smaller than Okta’s.

Bottom line: The default for cloud-born SMBs and AD-escaping mid-market alike.

3 Okta Universal Directory — Best Neutral Hub

Snapshot: Per-module [VERIFY] | Schema-flexible profiles | 7,000+ app catalog

Why it earns 3: The person-record hub for multi-source enterprises: HR, AD, and application profiles mastered into one schema-flexible record, serving as the central person-record hub across diverse HR and IAM directories that drives SSO and SCIM lifecycle automation across the largest independent catalog.

Standout features: Flexible schemas; source-of-truth rules; lifecycle automation; catalog reach; directory integrations.

Pros: Neutrality; lifecycle maturity.

Cons: Module pricing stacks; not a device manager.

Bottom line: The consolidation hub when no single ecosystem should own your identity.

4 Google Cloud Identity — Best Workspace-Native

Snapshot: Free + premium tiers (published) | Context-aware access | Passkey maturity

Why it earns 4: The Entra logic, Google edition: directory, SSO, and device basics bundled with Workspace, context-aware access from the BeyondCorp lineage, and industry-leading passkey posture that sets the standard for modern authentication defaults.

Standout features: Workspace-native directory; context-aware access; passkeys; MDM basics; published tiers.

Pros: Bundled; passkey pedigree; price floor.

Cons: Windows/legacy depth trails Entra; enterprise IGA thin.

Bottom line: Google-gravity organizations should exhaust this before shopping.

5 AWS Directory Service — Best Workload-AD Hosting

Snapshot: Published hourly by edition | Managed Microsoft AD | Lane label: workloads, not workforce

Why it earns 5: Real domain controllers as a service for EC2, RDS, and FSx workloads that still speak AD patched and replicated by AWS. It integrates natively with workload-level AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions while isolating underlying administrative infrastructure from directory enumeration.

Standout features: Managed Microsoft AD; trusts; AWS service integration; AD Connector; published pricing.

Pros: Removes DC ops; native AWS fit.

Cons: Not an end-user identity platform; always-on cost.

Bottom line: Lease it for stubborn workloads while your workforce directory lives elsewhere.

6 Ping Identity (incl. ForgeRock) — Best Federation-Scale Directory

Snapshot: Quote [VERIFY] | PingDirectory scale | One vendor since 2023

Why it earns 6: When the requirement reads “hundreds of millions of entries, five-nines, federation-heavy,” PingDirectory with ForgeRock’s directory heritage consolidated in is the specialist shortlist, fortified by vendor mitigations for high-scale federation and directory architectures. Ranked once despite two sheet entries.

Standout features: Massive-scale storage; sync/failover; LDAP/REST; CIAM pairing; hybrid deployment.

Pros: Scale ceiling.

Cons: Enterprise-only economics; identity-team prerequisite.

Bottom line: The national-scale answer; overkill below it.

7 OneLogin — Best Value Consolidation

Snapshot: Published per-user | Directory + SSO/MFA bundle | One Identity portfolio

Why it earns 7: Directory, SSO, and SmartFactor MFA on one transparent bill the mid-market play for replacing AD sprawl, reinforced by patches for OneLogin’s Active Directory Connector and cloud identity platform to ensure safe on-prem-to-cloud directory synchronization.

Standout features: Cloud directory; SSO/MFA; AD/HR sync; SCIM; desktop SSO.

Pros: Pricing transparency; quick rollout.

Cons: Catalog and momentum trail Okta.

Bottom line: The quote-free benchmark for mid-market consolidations.

8 Foxpass — Best RADIUS/LDAP Specialist

Snapshot: Published per-user | Cloud RADIUS/LDAP | Engineering-team favorite

Why it earns 8: Lane label: the protocol floor, productized. Foxpass delivers cloud RADIUS and LDAP Wi-Fi auth, VPN auth, server access syncing from Google, Okta, and Entra, while providing SSH key management and server access controls that engineering teams expense without friction.

Standout features: Cloud RADIUS/LDAP; SSH key management; IdP sync; API-first; published pricing.

Pros: Solves the cutover-killer; cheap; fast.

Cons: Not a full directory a protocol companion by design.

Bottom line: The bolt-on that saves domainless migrations from their Wi-Fi moment.

9 miniOrange — Best Budget Breadth

Snapshot: Published low per-user tiers | Directory + SSO/MFA + legacy connectors

Why it earns 9: The value long-tail: directory services plus SSO/MFA and unusually broad legacy-protocol connectors at the lowest published rates in this ranking, actively supported by vendor security updates for miniOrange identity and single sign-on connectors.

Standout features: Directory + IAM bundle; legacy protocol support; on-prem gateways; published tiers.

Pros: Price; integration long tail.

Cons: Enterprise polish and ecosystem depth.

Bottom line: The budget shortlist entry for odd-shaped estates.

Consolidated: ForgeRock — Ranked Within Ping (6)

ForgeRock’s directory and access products now sell under Ping Identity following the 2023 merger. Lists ranking them separately are counting one vendor twice we didn’t.

Full Comparison Table

Buying Advice: Inventory Before You Migrate

Three audits before any cutover: which apps still require AD (they decide whether AWS-hosted AD stays in the picture), which network gear needs RADIUS/LDAP (JumpCloud native or Foxpass bolt-on), and which system HR, IdP, or device tool masters the person record. Then set a retirement date for the last domain controller; without one, hybrid becomes permanent and you pay for both worlds indefinitely.

FAQs

What is the best cloud directory service in 2026? Entra ID ranks #1 on bundle gravity for Microsoft estates; JumpCloud leads the domainless package for SMB and mid-market; Okta Universal Directory is the best neutral multi-source hub; Google Cloud Identity wins Workspace-first shops.

Can a cloud directory fully replace Active Directory? Usually, gradually: cloud directory plus MDM plus passwordless authentication and FIDO2 passkeys covers most modern estates, with managed AD (AWS Directory Service) leased for stubborn legacy workloads. Application inventory not vendor capability sets the timeline.

What about Wi-Fi and VPN authentication? The classic cutover surprise: only some directories ship native RADIUS/LDAP (JumpCloud; Foxpass as specialist). Audit network-auth dependencies before signing, not during rollout week.

Are Ping Identity and ForgeRock separate directory vendors? No merged in 2023, one platform under Ping. Separate rankings double-count; evaluate the combined portfolio once.

Is AWS Directory Service a workforce directory? No it hosts AD-dependent workloads in AWS. Pair it with a workforce directory (Entra, JumpCloud, Okta); confusing the two lanes is the category’s most common buying error.

Verdict

Entra wins on gravity, JumpCloud on domainless completeness, Okta UD on neutrality and the best migrations treat all three audits (apps, protocols, person-record) as the real project.

Aligning your identity foundation with Zero Trust architecture principles ensures that every authenticated user, device, and network session is continuously validated.

The directory is decided by your estate; the retirement date for your last domain controller is decided by you.

Released on September 23 alongside Wireshark 4.4.19, the update is available as Windows and macOS installers and source code. Wireshark is the world’s most widely used network protocol analyzer, supporting packet-level […]

The post Wireshark 4.6.9 Fixes 19 Vulnerabilities Including Code Execution Via Malicious Packet appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Wireshark has released version 4.6.9, a security-focused update that addresses 19 documented vulnerabilities across protocol dissectors, capture-file parsers, the Sharkd utility, and configuration-profile handling. Released on September 23 alongside Wireshark 4.4.19, the update is available as Windows and macOS installers and source code.

Wireshark is the world’s most widely used network protocol analyzer, supporting packet-level troubleshooting, security analysis, software development, and education. Because analysts routinely open traffic captures and files collected from untrusted environments, flaws in the application’s parsing and dissection components can create a direct workstation risk, not merely interrupt an investigation.

Wireshark 4.6.9 Released

The most significant issue is CVE-2026-96419, tracked as wnpa-sec-2026-106. A specially crafted configuration profile can crash Wireshark or potentially execute arbitrary code when a user is persuaded to import it. The flaw affects Wireshark 4.6.0 through 4.6.8, and the 4.4 branch from 4.4.0 through 4.4.18; fixes are included in 4.6.9 and 4.4.19.

Wireshark’s advisory says it is unaware of active exploitation. However, the required user interaction does not eliminate the danger: a malicious profile could be delivered through phishing, a shared analysis package, a support case, or an untrusted repository and presented as a legitimate troubleshooting configuration.

The remaining advisories cover crashes, excessive loops, memory leaks, and denial-of-service conditions triggered while processing malformed data. Affected components include the ZigBee ZCL, SCTP, SPDY, CSN.1, MBIM, Frame, RF4CE, TIFF, X11, IEEE 802.11, Catapult DCT2000, USB HID, and IEEE C37.118 Synchrophasor dissectors. Parsers for TTL, PEAK CAN TRC, Microsoft Network Monitor, and Toshiba captures are also affected, while another flaw can crash Sharkd.

Several defects can consume resources without immediately terminating the application. The TTL and TIFF issues cause infinite loops, Microsoft Network Monitor parsing can enter a large loop, the Synchrophasor dissector leaks memory, and USB HID processing combines an infinite loop with a memory leak. Crafted captures could therefore hang analysis, exhaust resources, or disrupt automated pipelines.

Beyond the 19 CVE-backed advisories, Wireshark 4.6.9 corrects multiple security-relevant bugs. These include a DICOM heap overwrite caused by a 32-bit length wrap, LBMC fragment reassembly and Bluetooth AVCTP integer overflows, an SMB object-export integer overflow, a PKCS12 null-pointer dereference, and a stack-based buffer overflow in etwdump when parsing crafted ETL files.

The release notes also identify two separately tracked remote-code-execution bugs involving LBMC fragment reassembly and LoRaWAN decryption. Other fixes address out-of-bounds reads, an uninitialized buffer pointer, excessive DICOM memory amplification, and incorrect handling of GREASE values during JA4 fingerprint calculation.

These corrections matter to SOC teams because parser reliability and fingerprint accuracy directly affect triage, detection engineering, and forensic conclusions.

No new protocols were added. Wireshark updated support for technologies including QUIC, SMB, OpenFlow, DICOM, LoRaWAN, IEEE 802.11, X11, ZigBee ZCL, and SPDY, while capture-file updates cover BLF, Network Monitor, pcapng, PEAK TRC, Toshiba, and TTL.

Organizations should upgrade immediately to Wireshark 4.6.9 or, if remaining on the older maintenance branch, 4.4.19 or later. Until updates are deployed, analysts should avoid importing profiles or opening capture files from unverified sources, isolate risky analysis in a sandbox or disposable virtual machine, and restrict automated processing privileges.

Administrators should check analyst endpoints, jump boxes, forensic workstations, and centrally managed capture appliances. Official packages are available from Wireshark’s download page, which lists 4.6.9 as the stable release.

The flaws, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, each carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5 and can let remote, unauthenticated adversaries execute code, placing internet-facing gateways at immediate risk. The post Citrix Confirms NetScaler 0-Day RCE Vulnerabilities Actively Exploited in Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Citrix has released emergency security updates for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway after confirming that attackers are exploiting two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities against unmitigated appliances.

The flaws, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, each carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5 and can let remote, unauthenticated adversaries execute code, placing internet-facing gateways at immediate risk.

Because these appliances operate at the network edge and manage trusted traffic, a successful exploitation can create a strong foothold for lateral movement and credential theft.

The confirmation validates warnings covered yesterday by Cyber Security News, when watchTowr reported two previously undisclosed NetScaler RCE zero-days found during forensic investigations.

At that time, Citrix had not released CVE identifiers, affected builds, indicators of compromise, or patches, forcing some organizations to consider isolating exposed appliances while awaiting authoritative guidance.

NetScaler 0-Day RCE Exploited

CVE-2026-88771 results from improper input validation and can permit arbitrary command execution. Its exposure is unusually broad: every NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployment is affected, including default configurations, with no optional feature required.

CVE-2026-88772 is a memory-overflow flaw capable of causing RCE or denial of service when DTLS is enabled; DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers.

The bulletin addresses six additional vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-88773, rated 9.3, enables HTTP request smuggling in deployments using HTTP configurations.

CVE-2026-88774, scored 7.0, involves policy bypass through improper HTTP URL-based expressions, potentially allowing non-normalized URLs to evade WAF or security rules.

Three 8.8-rated memory-overflow flaws—CVE-2026-88775, CVE-2026-88776 and CVE-2026-88777—affect Gateway or AAA virtual servers, Oracle load-balancing virtual servers, and LB/CS or CGNAT-LSN/NAT64 devices using non-HTTP Layer 7 features, respectively.

CVE-2026-88778, also rated 8.8, permits TCP initial sequence number prediction when Enhanced ISN Generation is disabled on relevant TCP configurations.

Administrators should upgrade immediately to NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.37 or later, or 13.1-64.23 or later. Fixed specialized builds are 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 13.1-37.279 for FIPS and NDcPP deployments.

Because CVE-2026-88771 affects default installations, configuration-based exposure reduction cannot replace patching. Teams should still inspect configurations for DTLS, HTTP or SSL virtual servers, Gateway and AAA services, Oracle load balancing, non-HTTP Layer 7 protocols, and disabled Enhanced ISN Generation.

Citrix is providing generic indicators of compromise through NetScaler Console’s Security Advisory workflow. The capability requires telemetry and is available through the Console service and on-premises Console with Cloud Connect, beginning with version 14.1-73.36.

Citrix cautions that these checks cannot cover every attacker technique and may miss compromises; organizations finding suspicious activity should preserve evidence and engage qualified forensic responders. Logs should be forwarded to an external SIEM, while File Integrity Monitoring can help identify unauthorized changes.

A deployment running 13.1-64.23 may enter a reboot loop during upgrade when NetScaler variables are configured. Administrators can run show ns variable; if variables are returned, Citrix advises planning for 13.1-64.24. The Console may also temporarily mislabel 13.1-64.23 as vulnerable.

Given confirmed exploitation, defenders should treat the update as an incident-response priority, not routine patch management. Patch every node, verify the running build, scan for compromise, review authentication and network activity, and investigate unexpected files, processes, configuration changes or outbound connections.

Updating closes the vulnerabilities, but it does not remove persistence or other artifacts left by attackers who exploited an appliance before remediation.

articles.title: New Windows Process Injection Attack Evades EDR Monitoring Without WriteProcessMemory
articles.description:
A Windows process injection method disclosed by security researcher Two Seven One Three sidesteps two APIs closely associated with remote code injection: VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory. Dubbed console named-pipe injection, the technique delivers payload bytes through a child console process’s redirected standard input and repurposes memory Windows has already populated. It can disrupt detections built around […]

The post New Windows Process Injection Attack Evades EDR Monitoring Without WriteProcessMemory appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A Windows process injection method disclosed by security researcher Two Seven One Three sidesteps two APIs closely associated with remote code injection: VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory.

Dubbed console named-pipe injection, the technique delivers payload bytes through a child console process’s redirected standard input and repurposes memory Windows has already populated. It can disrupt detections built around the familiar allocate-write-execute sequence.

Process injection executes arbitrary code inside another process, potentially masking activity behind a legitimate application.

MITRE ATT&CK tracks the behavior as T1055, while conventional implementations commonly open or create a target, allocate remote memory, copy code with WriteProcessMemory, and start or hijack a thread. EDRs frequently correlate this chain’s memory and thread signals.

Windows Process Injection Evades EDR

The variation exploits Windows interprocess communication rather than a direct cross-process write. An injector creates an interactive console child, such as nslookup.exe or netsh.exe, redirects its standard input to a pipe, and sends the payload with WriteFile.

Microsoft documents that a parent can assign a pipe’s read end as a child’s standard-input handle and retain the opposite end for writing.

The bytes then exist in the console program’s address space as it processes input. The proof of concept prefixes the payload with a distinctive marker, searches accessible memory for that signature, and calculates the shellcode entry point beyond the marker.

The code image shows inheritable handles configured in STARTUPINFO, followed by CreateProcess with redirected streams.

After locating the buffer, the injector calls VirtualProtectEx to make the existing committed pages executable. It then suspends a thread, changes its instruction pointer, and resumes execution.

Microsoft says VirtualProtectEx changes protections in another process and requires PROCESS_VM_OPERATION; it recommends suspending a thread before changing its context.

Demonstration from security researcher Two Seven One Three output shows 368 bytes found inside an nslookup.exe region; its protection changed from read-write to executable-read-write, and the main thread was redirected to that address.

Payloads must avoid carriage return, line feed, and Ctrl+Z substitute bytes because console parsing may treat them as command terminators or end-of-file input. Memory discovery, remote protection changes, and thread-context manipulation also remain detectable.

Unlike related process-parameter poisoning research, this approach does not require launching the child suspended or placing unusually formatted data in command-line or environment fields.

SensePost researchers Max Hirschberger and Ogulcan Ugur said their separate technique bypassed four leading EDR products, but that does not validate this newer implementation.

Defenders should move beyond single-API alerts and correlate the complete behavior. High-value signals include an unusual parent launching an interactive console binary with redirected handles, binary-like standard-input writes, memory scanning, a remote VirtualProtectEx transition to executable permissions, and SetThreadContext followed by resumption.

Sysmon Event IDs 17 and 18 provide named-pipe telemetry, although anonymous standard-input pipes may require richer endpoint and handle-level visibility.

Security teams should baseline console automation and hunt for rare combinations rather than flagging every conhost.exe, nslookup.exe, or pipe operation.

Research shows an important lesson for engineering tools that detect harmful process injections. Reliable detection requires looking at how processes are created, how handles are shared, how memory is protected, and how control flows change. It shouldn’t rely on a single method.

articles.description:

However, Citrix had not published technical details, CVE identifiers, affected builds, indicators of compromise, […]

The post Citrix NetScaler 0-Day RCE Vulnerabilities Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Citrix NetScaler administrators are confronting reports of two undisclosed remote code execution vulnerabilities allegedly exploited in real-world attacks.

watchTowr said the flaws are unpatched zero-days, were identified during forensic investigations, and that Citrix communications and fixes are expected early next week. However, Citrix had not published technical details, CVE identifiers, affected builds, indicators of compromise, or an advisory for these reported flaws at the time of writing, leaving defenders to make high-impact decisions with limited verified information.

The warning began with reports that multiple unpatched NetScaler RCE vulnerabilities were circulating in the wild. watchTowr described the intelligence as credible and later stated that two separate vulnerabilities can enable remote code execution.

The company has not publicly disclosed exploitation paths, prerequisites, payloads, or forensic artifacts, making independent validation difficult. Treat the claims as a serious warning, not yet a fully vendor-confirmed disclosure.

Some organizations reportedly responded by shutting down internet-exposed NetScaler appliances. Such action can interrupt VPN access, application delivery, authentication, and other critical services, yet edge appliances occupy a privileged position at the network boundary.

If defenders cannot patch or reliably mitigate a potentially exploitable RCE flaw, temporarily removing exposed systems from service may be the safer decision, particularly for sensitive environments.

The emerging alert must not be confused with Citrix’s August 19 bulletin covering CVE-2026-19490 and CVE-2026-19489. CVE-2026-19490 is a critical authentication-bypass flaw rated 9.3 under CVSS v4.0; it affects certain customer-managed NetScaler Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations.

CVE-2026-19489, rated 8.8, is a memory-overflow issue requiring SIP ALG on a Large Scale NAT group and can cause unpredictable behavior or denial of service.

Active exploitation of CVE-2026-19490 is already established. Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency warned on September 7 that exploitation attempts had been observed, while CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 9. Canada’s Cyber Center subsequently urged emergency patching and monitoring for unauthorized access.

Those facts fueled uncertainty over whether the latest alarm concerned the known authentication bypass or genuinely new zero-days; watchTowr’s later wording explicitly characterized the reported issues as two unpatched RCE flaws.

For the August vulnerabilities, Citrix advises upgrading NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 to 14.1-73.32 or later and 13.1 to 13.1-63.21 or later. Fixed baselines for specialized editions are 14.1-73.32 FIPS and 13.1-37.277 for FIPS or NDcPP. Citrix lists no workaround for those flaws, and its bulletin applies to customer-managed appliances rather than Citrix-managed cloud services.

Until Citrix clarifies the new RCE reports, defenders should inventory every NetScaler instance, confirm exact builds and exposure, restrict management access, and place compensating controls before public interfaces.

Security teams should preserve logs and forensic images, review authentication events, new sessions, configuration changes, unexpected processes, suspicious files, and anomalous outbound connections, and avoid wiping potentially compromised devices before collecting evidence.

Organizations unable to accept the residual risk should isolate or shut down exposed appliances under an approved business-continuity process. Teams should also monitor Citrix’s security bulletin channel for patches and deployment guidance rather than relying on social-media fragments alone.

The episode again shows why internet-facing remote-access infrastructure demands rapid asset discovery, tested emergency patching, centralized logging, and rehearsed incident-response procedures, especially when defenders must act before complete technical disclosure arrives.

articles.title: Which Platforms to Use for Enterprise Threat Intelligence
articles.description:
Enterprise threat intelligence calls for a platform that filters the flood of global threat data down to what is relevant to a specific organization, draws on collection broad enough to surface threats before they appear publicly, ties activity to the actors and exploited vulnerabilities behind it, and correlates those signals into an evidence-backed view of […]

The post Which Platforms to Use for Enterprise Threat Intelligence appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Enterprise threat intelligence calls for a platform that filters the flood of global threat data down to what is relevant to a specific organization, draws on collection broad enough to surface threats before they appear publicly, ties activity to the actors and exploited vulnerabilities behind it, and correlates those signals into an evidence-backed view of risk. 

Commodity feeds report every global threat; an enterprise platform reports the ones that matter to you.

CloudSEK is one provider built for this work, combining threat actor tracking, exploited-vulnerability intelligence, and collection across surface, deep, and dark web sources with correlation against an organization’s own exposure.

Choosing well matters because the difference between platforms is not the volume of data they ingest but whether that data becomes a decision a security team can act on before an adversary moves.

What Enterprise Threat Intelligence Requires

At enterprise scale, the challenge is rarely a shortage of threat data. It is the opposite: an excess of feeds, alerts, and indicators that a security team cannot manually reconcile into a clear view of its own risk.

An enterprise threat intelligence platform earns its place by resolving that excess into relevance. Five capabilities determine whether a platform achieves this.

  • Breadth and depth of collection. Enterprise-relevant intelligence draws on surface, deep, and dark web sources, underground forums, code repositories, paste sites, and technical telemetry. Narrow collection produces a narrow, and often misleading, picture of the threat landscape.
  • Relevance filtering. A feed that reports every global threat is noise. A platform that maps threats to an organization’s industry, geography, technology stack, and known exposure delivers intelligence a team can prioritize.
  • Actor and campaign context. Indicators alone age quickly. Tying activity to the threat actors, tactics, techniques, and procedures behind it produces intelligence that remains useful as infrastructure rotates.
  • Exploited-vulnerability tracking. With tens of thousands of CVEs disclosed annually and only a small fraction ever exploited, a platform that identifies which vulnerabilities are under active exploitation is what makes risk-based patching possible.
  • Correlation and integration. Intelligence delivers value only when it reaches the systems that act on it. A platform that correlates its findings and feeds them into existing detection, response, and vulnerability-management workflows turns intelligence into operational capability.

Capabilities That Distinguish Platforms

Every vendor in this space markets threat intelligence. Four distinctions determine enterprise value.

Relevance Over Volume

A defining test of an enterprise platform is whether it reduces noise or adds to it. A high volume of alerts is not a measure of quality; a smaller set of findings tied directly to the organization’s sector, assets, and exposure is far more valuable to a team that must act on a finite budget of analyst time.

Collection Beyond Open Sources

Much of the most consequential threat activity, leaked credentials, initial-access sales, exploit trading, and campaign coordination, occurs in deep and dark web spaces that open-source feeds never reach. 

Platforms that collect across these sources often surface an emerging threat before it appears in the open, giving enterprises the lead time they need.

Correlation Across the Threat Surface

An exposed asset, a leaked credential, an exploited CVE, and a threat actor’s known activity can each appear as a separate signal. 

A platform that correlates them into a single, attributed picture converts isolated data points into an understanding of who is targeting the organization and how. That correlation is often the practical difference between a data subscription and an intelligence capability.

Evidence and Confidence

Enterprise decisions carry weight, so the reasoning behind an intelligence finding matters as much as the finding itself.

Strong platforms expose their sources and evidence, allowing analysts to weigh a conclusion rather than accept it on trust, and to communicate risk to leadership with a defensible basis.

How CloudSEK Delivers Enterprise Threat Intelligence

CloudSEK Threat Intelligence is built to resolve the enterprise excess of threat data into relevance, which is what separates it from a commodity feed.

Actor and TTP tracking. It tracks threat actors and their tactics, techniques, and procedures, along with the malware and ransomware campaigns associated with them, so intelligence stays useful as an actor’s infrastructure rotates.

Exploited-vulnerability intelligence. It identifies the vulnerabilities under active exploitation, tying a threat not only to past activity but to the specific weaknesses attackers are using now, which is what makes risk-based patching possible.

Underground collection. Its collection extends across surface, deep, and dark web sources, bringing underground activity, leaked-credential exposure, and exploit discussion into the intelligence picture rather than relying on open sources alone. This is frequently where an emerging threat surfaces first.

Correlation against the organization’s own risk. Because CloudSEK Threat Intelligence operates alongside CloudSEK’s broader digital risk and attack surface capabilities, an external threat can be correlated with an organization’s own exposure, leaked credentials, exposed assets, or infrastructure referencing the organization.

CloudSEK Nexus AI connects these signals into a validated view rather than presenting each as an isolated alert, so intelligence is grounded in the enterprise’s actual risk rather than delivered in the abstract.

How to Evaluate an Enterprise Threat Intelligence Platform

Assess every shortlisted platform against the same criteria, using the organization’s own sector, technology stack, and threat history rather than a generic demonstration.

Evaluate outcomes rather than feed size. A platform that surfaces fewer but more relevant, better-evidenced findings serves an enterprise better than one that maximizes volume without context.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a threat feed and a threat intelligence platform?

A threat feed delivers raw indicators, IPs, hashes, and domains, without context or prioritization. A threat intelligence platform filters, correlates, and contextualizes that data against an organization’s own exposure, turning indicators into decisions a team can act on.

What makes threat intelligence “enterprise-grade”? 

Enterprise-grade intelligence is defined by relevance filtering, breadth of collection including deep and dark web sources, actor and campaign context, exploited-vulnerability tracking, and correlation into existing workflows, rather than by the raw volume of data delivered.

Why does dark web collection matter for enterprise threat intelligence? 

Leaked credentials, initial-access sales, exploit trading, and campaign coordination often occur in deep and dark web spaces before the resulting activity appears in the open. Collection across these sources gives an enterprise lead time that open-source feeds cannot.

How does threat intelligence support vulnerability management? 

By identifying which CVEs are under active exploitation, threat intelligence lets a security team prioritize the small fraction of vulnerabilities attackers are actually using, rather than patching by severity score alone.

Conclusion

The right enterprise threat intelligence platform filters the flood of global threat data down to what is relevant to the organization, draws on collection broad enough to see threats before they surface publicly, ties activity to the actors and exploited vulnerabilities behind it, and correlates those signals into a clear, evidence-backed view of risk.

At enterprise scale, the decisive quality is not the size of the feed but the relevance of the intelligence and the speed with which it reaches the teams that act on it.

Platforms built to resolve data into relevance, including CloudSEK, should be evaluated against the organization’s own threat profile, because the only intelligence that delivers enterprise value is intelligence grounded in the threats that genuinely target the organization.

articles.title: Local AI Model Modifies Windows Credential Dumper to Bypass EDR Detection
articles.description:
A locally hosted, uncensored artificial intelligence model modified a Windows credential-dumping utility until it evaded two Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) products in a controlled lab, highlighting how accessible generative AI could accelerate custom offensive-tool development. The experiment, published by Project Black researcher Eddie Zhang, targeted the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS), whose memory […]

The post Local AI Model Modifies Windows Credential Dumper to Bypass EDR Detection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A locally hosted, uncensored artificial intelligence model modified a Windows credential-dumping utility until it evaded two Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) products in a controlled lab, highlighting how accessible generative AI could accelerate custom offensive-tool development.

The experiment, published by Project Black researcher Eddie Zhang, targeted the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS), whose memory may contain authentication material useful for lateral movement after an attacker obtains administrative access.

The project began with a deliberately challenging benchmark: could an AI create an executable capable of dumping LSASS without modern EDR detecting it, while requiring little human direction? This is a consequential test because MITRE ATT&CK tracks LSASS memory dumping as T1003.001, a Credential Access sub-technique. Administrative or SYSTEM-level users can harvest credentials from LSASS memory and reuse them to authenticate to additional systems.

According to Zhang, attempts to generate the dumper with Claude Opus 5, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 5 produced immediate refusals, despite his organization’s approval under Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

He then tested the open-weight DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 model. After several prompts, DeepSeek produced a functioning executable that accepted a process identifier, created a suspended clone of the target through reflection, generated an in-memory minidump, XOR-encrypted it, and wrote the encrypted output to disk.

The researcher validated the resulting dump with pypykatz, confirming it could be parsed, but the initial executable still triggered EDR detection. When asked to improve stealth, DeepSeek invoked a safety guardrail.

Zhang therefore moved the code to an uncensored, community-modified Qwen 3.8 27B model, running locally on a password-cracking rig equipped with two Nvidia RTX 4090 graphics cards.

Local AI Bypasses EDR

With only a request to make the executable “more stealthy,” the local model returned a revised build that generated no detections across either of the two EDR platforms available in the lab, Zhang reported.

Code review showed that Qwen had altered process-spawning behavior, reduced access masks requested against the target process, inserted randomized delays during minidump construction, changed the output filename and path, and scrubbed embedded strings from the binary.

Those modifications matter because many defenses correlate recognizable artifacts: suspicious process ancestry, high-privilege handle requests to LSASS, known strings, dump-file creation, and tightly timed behavior.

Elastic, for example, documents a tool-agnostic rule that monitors LSASS handle requests with access masks frequently used by dump utilities, while MITRE describes detection through a sequence of abnormal process access followed by memory dumping or file creation.

The finding is significant, but its scope remains limited. The EDR vendors were not named, configuration details were not published, and success against two laboratory products does not establish universal bypass capability.

It nevertheless shows how local, guardrail-free models can iteratively reshape known offensive code without sending prompts or source code to a hosted service, lowering the expertise and time needed to produce environment-specific variants.

Defenders should treat EDR as one layer rather than a guarantee. Microsoft recommends enabling the LSASS credential-stealing Attack Surface Reduction rule with tamper protection, running LSASS as Protected Process Light, deploying Credential Guard, restricting RDP administration, and disabling WDigest credential caching.

Organizations should also minimize local administrator rights, separate privileged accounts, use unique credentials, monitor unusual LSASS access, and rapidly isolate hosts showing credential-dumping behavior.
